body:
What is artificial intelligence?

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science concerned with developing systems that can perform tasks normally associated with human intelligence. These tasks include recognising patterns, understanding language, making predictions, solving problems and selecting suitable actions.

For example, a computer system may recognise spoken words, suggest a translation, identify an object in a photograph or recommend learning material based on a student's progress. The system processes information and produces an output suited to the task.

Artificial intelligence: The development of computer systems capable of performing tasks that ordinarily require abilities such as learning, reasoning, perception or language understanding.

AI does not necessarily possess human consciousness, emotions or common sense. A system can perform a particular task very effectively while remaining unreliable in situations different from those for which it was developed.

AI and ordinary computer automation

Not every automated computer program uses AI. A traditional program generally follows instructions written explicitly by a programmer. For example, a school fee system may automatically add a fixed late fee whenever payment occurs after the due date. The system follows a predefined rule rather than learning from examples.

An AI-based system may instead examine patterns in previous records to estimate which fee reminders are most likely to be useful. It produces predictions using information learned from data. However, AI is broader than machine learning: some AI systems also use explicitly written rules and logical reasoning.

Relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning

Machine learning (ML) is a major part of AI in which a computer system learns patterns from data rather than relying entirely on manually written rules. The trained system can then make predictions or produce other outputs for new inputs.

Deep learning is a part of machine learning that uses neural networks with multiple processing layers. It is especially important in many modern image, speech and language applications.

The relationship is important because the terms are not interchangeable. A rule-based expert system may use AI without machine learning. A simple spam classifier may use machine learning without deep learning. Many modern image-recognition systems use deep learning.

Where AI is useful

  • Education: Supporting language translation, reading assistance, personalised practice and identification of learning difficulties.
  • Agriculture: Helping analyse crop photographs, weather information and other observations to support decisions.
  • Healthcare: Assisting professionals in examining medical images or organising information, subject to clinical verification.
  • Public services: Supporting document processing, translation, information retrieval and responses to routine enquiries.
  • Transport: Supporting route suggestions, traffic-pattern analysis and driver-assistance functions.

In each case, usefulness depends on the quality of the system, its data and the conditions under which it is used. A tool intended to assist a decision is not automatically suitable for making that decision without human review.

A historical foundation

The term artificial intelligence was introduced by John McCarthy in a 1955 proposal for a research meeting. The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, held in 1956 in the United States, is widely regarded as a founding event in the development of AI as a field of study.

Prelims focus

  • AI is the broad field concerned with intelligent computer behaviour.
  • Machine learning is a part of AI that learns patterns from data.
  • Deep learning is a part of machine learning based on multilayer neural networks.
  • John McCarthy introduced the term artificial intelligence in a 1955 proposal.
  • The Dartmouth AI research project took place in 1956.
  • Trap: Every automated computer program is not necessarily an AI system, and every AI system does not use deep learning.

[Sources: Google for Developers, Introduction to Machine Learning, 'What is Machine Learning?' (consulted 4 November 2026); Computer History Museum, 'John McCarthy,' PDP-1 Restoration Project, biographical section (consulted 4 November 2026); Dartmouth College, 'The Founding and Future of AI,' 'Where AI Was Born' and 'Defining a Field' (consulted 4 November 2026).]

title: Artificial Intelligence: Meaning, Scope and Everyday Applications

body:
Learning from examples

A machine-learning system improves its ability to perform a task by finding useful patterns in data. Instead of giving the computer a separate rule for every possible situation, developers provide examples and a method for learning from them.

Consider an email-filtering system. A conventional program might block every message containing one particular word. Such a rule could wrongly block an important message or fail to detect an unwanted message that uses different words. A machine-learning system can examine many examples of emails and learn combinations of features associated with unwanted messages.

Data, features and labels

A dataset is a collection of information used for a task. Each example may contain several features, meaning characteristics that help the system make a prediction. In an email example, features might include the sender's address, words in the message or the presence of a suspicious link.

In supervised learning, training examples also include labels. A label gives the known answer for an example. For an email-filtering task, labels might be 'spam' and 'not spam'.

Feature means information used to make a prediction. Label means the known answer supplied during supervised training. The features help the model predict the label.

What happens during training?

Training is the process through which a machine-learning method adjusts a model using training data. A model is the resulting system that has learned patterns useful for the task. An algorithm is the method used to perform the learning or computation; the trained model is the result of that learning process.

For example, an email model may learn that an unusual sender address combined with certain message patterns is associated with spam. The relationship is learned from examples rather than being individually specified for every email.

Testing and generalisation

Learning the training examples is not enough. The real purpose is to perform well on new, previously unseen data. This ability is called generalisation.

Developers therefore evaluate a model using examples not used to train it. A model that performs well on training examples but poorly on new examples may suffer from overfitting. It has learned details of the training data that do not work reliably in other situations.

Good testing must reflect the real conditions in which the model will be used. An email filter tested only on old messages may perform poorly when the wording of unwanted emails changes.

Inference: using the trained model

Inference occurs when a trained model processes a new input and produces a prediction or another output. For example, after training, the spam filter examines a newly received email and predicts whether it is unwanted.

Training and inference are different activities. During training, the system learns or adjusts patterns. During ordinary inference, it uses those learned patterns without automatically retraining itself after every prediction. Some systems are designed to update through later training or feedback, but this must not be assumed for every AI tool.

Why data quality matters

A model can be unreliable if its examples are inaccurate, outdated, too few or unrepresentative of the people and situations it will encounter. Training on a large amount of data does not guarantee accuracy if important groups or conditions are missing.

Prelims focus

  • A dataset contains examples used for a machine-learning task.
  • Features are input characteristics; labels are known answers in supervised learning.
  • Training adjusts a model using data.
  • Inference uses the trained model to produce an output for a new input.
  • Generalisation means performing well on previously unseen data.
  • Trap: High accuracy on training examples alone does not prove that a model will work well on new examples.

[Sources: Google for Developers, Introduction to Machine Learning, 'Supervised Learning' and 'What is Machine Learning?' (consulted 4 November 2026); Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, 'Overfitting' (consulted 4 November 2026).]

title: How Machine Learning Works: Data, Training, Testing and Inference

body:
Why machine learning has different approaches

Machine-learning problems differ according to the information available and what the system is expected to learn. A school may want to predict an examination result, group students with similar learning needs or develop a program that improves its actions through feedback. These tasks do not require the same learning approach.

Supervised learning: examples with known answers

Supervised learning uses labelled examples. Each example contains input information and a known target answer. During training, the model learns a relationship that can help predict answers for new examples.

Two common supervised-learning tasks are:

  • Classification: Predicting a category or class. Examples include identifying an email as spam or not spam, or classifying a photograph as showing a cat or a dog.
  • Regression: Predicting a numerical value. Examples include estimating a house price or predicting the amount of rainfall from relevant measurements.

Classification and regression are not two completely separate families of AI. They are common tasks within supervised learning. The distinction concerns the kind of answer: a category or a number.

If past records contain study hours and known examination marks, a model trained to estimate a student's numerical marks is performing a regression task. If the model instead predicts whether the student belongs to a 'needs additional support' or 'does not need additional support' category, it is performing classification.

Unsupervised learning: finding patterns without supplied answers

Unsupervised learning examines data without known target labels for each example. It searches for patterns, similarities or structures in the available information.

A common example is clustering, which groups similar items. A school might group learning materials according to similarities in their content without first assigning every item a subject label. The computer discovers the groupings, while people may later examine what those groups mean.

An important limitation is that a cluster is not automatically a meaningful or correct category. Grouping similar data points does not prove that the groups correspond to an established classification.

Reinforcement learning: learning through rewards

Reinforcement learning (RL) involves an agent that selects actions in an environment. The agent receives a reward or penalty-related feedback depending on what happens. Over repeated interactions, it learns which actions are more likely to produce desirable outcomes.

For example, a simple computer-game agent may learn to avoid obstacles and reach a goal. Successful actions may receive positive rewards, while unsuccessful actions receive lower rewards or penalties. Unlike supervised learning, the agent is not necessarily shown the correct action for every situation.

Comparing the approaches

ApproachInformation availableMain purposeSimple example
Supervised learningInputs with known labelsPredict categories or numbersSpam detection
Unsupervised learningInputs without target labelsFind patterns or groupsGrouping similar documents
Reinforcement learningFeedback from actionsLearn useful decisions over timeGame agent learning to reach a goal

These approaches describe how learning is organised. They are not necessarily mutually exclusive in a complex AI system, but a basic question can usually be solved by identifying whether the example provides known answers, unlabelled data or rewards from actions.

Prelims focus

  • Supervised learning uses labelled examples.
  • Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a numerical value.
  • Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabelled data.
  • Clustering is a common unsupervised-learning task.
  • Reinforcement learning involves an agent, actions, an environment and rewards.
  • Trap: A reward for an action is not the same thing as a known correct label attached to every training example.

[Sources: Google for Developers, Introduction to Machine Learning, 'What is Machine Learning?,' sections 'Supervised learning,' 'Unsupervised learning' and 'Reinforcement learning' (consulted 4 November 2026); Google for Developers, Introduction to Machine Learning, 'Supervised Learning' (consulted 4 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Reinforcement learning uses the results of actions to improve future choices.

title: Three Main Learning Approaches: Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning

body:
How a neural network recognises patterns

An artificial neural network is a machine-learning model made of connected processing units, often called artificial neurons or nodes. Information passes through these units, and the network learns useful relationships by adjusting connections during training.

The name is inspired by biological neurons, but an artificial neural network is a mathematical computer model. It should not be treated as a complete reproduction of the human brain.

In a simple image-recognition example, the input may be a photograph of a crop leaf. The network processes visual information and produces an output, such as the estimated category of the leaf's condition. The prediction is based on patterns learned from earlier examples.

What makes deep learning different?

Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple processing layers. These layers can learn increasingly useful patterns from data. For image recognition, early processing may respond to simple visual features, while later processing can combine information associated with more complex shapes or objects.

Deep-learning methods are widely used in speech recognition, image analysis and modern language systems. However, not all machine-learning models use neural networks, and a deep-learning system is not automatically more suitable for every small or simple problem.

Matching applications to suitable tasks

AI is useful when information contains patterns that can help achieve a defined goal. The choice of system depends on the task:

  • Recognising images: A trained model may identify objects or possible signs of crop damage in a photograph.
  • Recognising speech: An AI system may convert spoken words into text. Its accuracy can vary with background noise, accent and language.
  • Translating language: AI may produce a translation that helps communication, but technical terms, context and local expressions still need checking.
  • Making predictions: AI may estimate a numerical value from relevant past observations, but unexpected conditions can reduce accuracy.
  • Generating content: A generative model may draft text or create images, which must be reviewed for accuracy and appropriateness.

An agricultural example

Suppose a farmer photographs a leaf showing unusual spots. A trained image model may compare its visual patterns with those learned from earlier labelled photographs and suggest a possible category. This could help decide whether further examination is needed.

However, similar marks may have different causes. Lighting, camera quality, crop variety and local conditions can affect the result. A photograph alone may not provide enough information to recommend a treatment. Local observations and qualified human assessment remain important.

A model's prediction is not the same as a verified diagnosis. Even a system that performs well in testing can make mistakes when it encounters unfamiliar data or conditions.

General limitations

AI systems may fail because of poor training data, insufficient examples, unfamiliar inputs, changing conditions or inappropriate use. Some models require substantial computing resources, and their predictions may be difficult to explain. Reliability therefore has to be evaluated for the particular use rather than assumed from the name of the technology.

Prelims focus

  • Artificial neural networks are machine-learning models with connected processing units.
  • Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple processing layers.
  • Image recognition, speech recognition and language applications are important uses of deep learning.
  • AI performance depends on the quality and relevance of its training data.
  • Trap: A probable AI classification does not establish the actual cause of a crop disease or another real-world condition.

[Sources: Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course, 'Neural Networks' and 'Overfitting' (consulted 4 November 2026); Google for Developers, Introduction to Machine Learning, 'What is Machine Learning?' (consulted 4 November 2026).]
